title: Application Authentication and OAuth
description: Understand how OAuth 2.0 lets applications authenticate users without handling passwords.

data.text: In the past, apps asked for your username and password directly. That was risky — the app could misuse your credentials. OAuth 2.0 fixes this by letting users grant limited access without sharing secrets.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It uses access tokens — short-lived strings that prove an app has permission to act on behalf of a user.

data.title: OAuth 2.0 Grant Types
items: Authorization Code — best for web apps
Client Credentials — best for service-to-service calls
Implicit — older, avoid for new apps
Device Code — for devices without browsers
Refresh Token — silently renews access without user interaction

data.title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow (Conceptual)
data.content: The app redirects the user to Entra ID. After login, Entra ID redirects back with a code. The app exchanges the code for an access token.

data.caption: How the Authorization Code flow moves data between the app, browser, and Entra ID.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as App
    participant E as Entra ID
    U->>A: Click "Sign in"
    A->>E: Redirect to /authorize
    E->>U: Show login & consent
    U->>E: Enter credentials
    E->>A: Redirect with auth code
    A->>E: POST /token with code
    E->>A: Return access token
    A->>E: Call API with access token

data.text: OAuth 2.0 issues access tokens. OpenID Connect, which sits on top of OAuth 2.0, adds an ID token. They are not interchangeable. An access token is meant for an API: its audience is the API, and it carries scopes or app roles. An ID token is meant for the client application: its audience is the client ID, and it proves that the user authenticated. Sending an ID token to your API, or trusting an access token as proof of a user identity without validating it, is a common and serious mistake.

data.text: Authorization Code flow with PKCE in code

The Authorization Code flow is the default for web apps, desktop apps, and single-page apps. Public clients such as SPAs and desktop apps must use PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) instead of a client secret, because they cannot keep a secret. data.title: Common OAuth mistakes
items: Using the implicit flow for new applications. It returns tokens in the URL fragment and is no longer recommended.
Storing tokens in localStorage in a browser app. Any XSS bug can read them; prefer secure, HTTP-only cookies with a backend-for-frontend.
Forgetting to validate the state parameter, which enables login CSRF.
Requesting broad scopes such as User.ReadWrite.All when a single delegated scope is enough.
Hardcoding a client secret in a SPA. Public clients use PKCE, not secrets.

data.title: What interviewers look for
data.text: Expect to be asked "authentication versus authorization" and "ID token versus access token". A strong answer also mentions consent, scopes, and the fact that the resource server, not the client, must validate the token. Naming PKCE for public clients is a clear senior signal.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: OAuth 2.0 is about delegation, not authentication alone.
Access tokens prove an app has permission to act for a user.
The Authorization Code flow is the recommended approach for web apps.
